newsitem.title: NORWAY: FOCUS-Norway's Hydro jumps on Q-1 profits.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Norway's Hydro jumps on Q-1 profits.

text.p: Shares in Norsk Hydro ASA, Norway's largest listed company, soared on Monday following the release of first-quarter profits, which beat market forecasts.
The net income fell 18 percent to 1.54 billion crowns ($219 million) from 1.87 billion in the same ago period a year ago, but it surpassed analysts' consensus expectations by about five percent.
The industrial conglomerate's stock was traded at 349 crowns per share in the early afternoon on the Oslo Bourse, up 17 crowns from the opening.
"After a slight setback at the end of 1996, we're pleased to say that Hydro is back on the right track," Chief Executive Officer Egil Mylebust said.
"However, the months ahead do hold some potential uncertainties in the world economy and in the market prospects for the major sectors in which Hydro operates," he said.
Operating revenues rose by nearly nine percent to 23.25 billion crowns and operating income increased marginally to 3.15 billion. Earnings per share were 6.70 crowns, down from 8.20.
Hydro said in a statement that weaker earnings in agricultural operations and higher calculated tax on oil and gas income burdened first-quarter profits.

At the same time, agriculture was the most positive surprise in the accounts with an operating income of 856 million crowns. It was four percent less than in the first quarter last year, which was the best in the division's history, but it was 20 percent higher than market forecasts.
Hydro said fertiliser sales were particularly high near the end of the quarter, but earnings were weaker because of lower fertiliser prices and increased costs for raw materials.
Hydro's fertiliser sales to the important European markets increased by 30 percent primarily thanks to the acquisition of the Italian fertiliser operations from ENI, it said.
But it forecast new capacity in the world was expected to put downward pressure on the prices of urea and ammonia.
"Agriculture points in the right direction and we will upgrade our expectations of that division," an Oslo-based analyst said.

"But on the whole the market reaction is a bit too positive because the results do not herald a new trend. Nothing happens in terms of volume in Oil and Gas. They have simply been good at selling forward before the prices fell," the analyst said.

First-quarter operating income for Oil and Gas was 1.92 billion, up from 1.50 billion, thanks primarily to a crude oil price of $21.4/bbl and higher production and lower operating costs per barrel than before, Hydro said.
It said the outlook for oil prices was uncertain.

The operating income for Light Metals fell to 396 million crowns from 689 million principally because of lower aluminium prices. But the operating income for aluminium showed significant improvement over the fourth quarter of 1996, the statement said.
New industry capacity, and the potential start-up of idled smelters, may offset the effect of increased demand for aluminium, it said.

Petrochemicals' operating income shrank to 59 million crowns from 87 million. The weaker performance was due to lower caustic soda prices, higher raw materials costs as well as reduced output and sales due to the phase-in of new polyvinylchloride (PVC) production capacity in Norway and Britain.

Vice President and Chief Financial Officer Leiv Nergaard said the Hydro Plus improvement initiative, which was concluded at the end of 1996, provided a new platform for further growth. Results were already evident during 1996 in the form of a higher rate of investment and the acquisition of several businesses, he told Hydro's in-house magazine Profile.

"We're already seeing the impact of these changes in the first quarter, particularly in Agriculture. The Italian fertilizer operations which we acquired, coupled with the expansion of our marketing capacity in central Europe and on other continents, have compensated for the negative developments in the western European fertilizer markets, where low price has been a major factor," Nergaard said. ($ = 7.021 Norwegian Crowns)
